Consult Summary:
- Remote consult for 2–3 days of exertional shortness of breath with wheeze and cough in a patient with known asthma; likely mild asthma exacerbation; interim inhaler adjustments and urgent in-person review advised.

History:
- Presenting complaint: 2–3 days of shortness of breath (noticed while running; now also with brisk walking), wheeze, and cough; blue inhaler provided little relief.
- Associated symptoms: No sputum.
- Pertinent negatives: No medication allergies. No prior asthma-related hospital admissions. No prior oral steroids recalled.
- Asthma history: Last asthma attack 3–4 years ago. Last asthma review ~2 years ago. Not checking peak flow during current symptoms; usual peak flow reportedly ~380 (units not documented; patient agreed to clinician’s estimate).
- Medications:
  - Salbutamol (blue inhaler) used as needed and also in mornings/evenings “to prevent” symptoms; dose/route/frequency not fully documented.
  - Preventer inhaler: Brown inhaler identified by clinician as Clenil; patient reports using it twice daily; baseline dose not confirmed.
  - Cetraben and hydrocortisone (topicals) for skin symptoms; doses/routes/frequencies not documented.
- Allergies: Hay fever (environmental). No medication allergies reported.
- Family history: Brother with asthma; sister with eczema.
- Social/preventive: Physically active (runs). No other social history discussed.

Examination:


Impression:
- Asthma with probable mild exacerbation over the last 2–3 days; currently managed at home; needs face-to-face assessment.

Plan:
- Medication adjustments (interim):
  - Increase brown preventer (Clenil) to 4 puffs twice daily while awaiting review.
  - Use blue inhaler (salbutamol) as needed; advised up to every 2–4 hours (later stated “every two hourly”); frequent need indicates poor control.
- Safety/ED precautions:
  - If breathing worsens, or if needing frequent blue inhaler use, attend Emergency Department (A&E) and do not wait for clinic appointment.
- Follow-up:
  - Book a face-to-face GP appointment within the next few days for chest exam and peak flow measurement; treatment (e.g., oral steroids and/or antibiotics) to be considered based on findings.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: Exact medication names/brands and doses for preventer and reliever; inhaler technique and spacer use; smoking status/exposure; triggers; vitals and respiratory exam; current peak flow; written asthma action plan; vaccination status (influenza/COVID).  
● Internal conflicts: 
  - Medication list initially included “Bactroban,” later corrected to “Cetraben” (conflict noted). 
  - Preventer named by clinician as “Clenil”; earlier patient said “Flanel” (name unclear). 
  - Salbutamol frequency guidance stated as “every 2–4 hours” and later “every two hourly” (minor inconsistency).  
● Transcript quality: Several unclear/inaudible segments and misheard medication names; some clinician-prompted values (peak flow) accepted by patient.
